solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Inferior multinational company corrupting influencer

parts.note: goods of inferior quality are bad goods, the plainest word for it
the Californian computer and phone maker, one of the largest multinationals there is

explanation.surface: A shoddy global corporation shaping what people think.
explanation.walkthrough: Influencer reads as the person paid to hold products up to a phone camera; the wordplay wants the older sense, anyone whose presence works on those around them. The company is the one with the fruit on the lid.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad apple is the one in the barrel that rots the rest, so the phrase names whoever spoils the company he is put in.

clue.text: Inhabitant: "Good for Macron to import right computer networks etc"

indicators.note: To import is to bring goods in from outside, so the word before it opens and takes what follows inside.

parts.note: bon is French for good, and Macron is the French president; the word parts after its first letter
R is right, as on a map or in a stage direction
IT is information technology, the department that runs the computers and the networks between them

explanation.surface: A French verdict that the president should be buying his technology in.
explanation.walkthrough: Macron is there to set you thinking in French, where good is bon. The quotation marks keep the whole second half sounding like a line from a politician rather than a set of instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A Briton is an inhabitant of Britain, the noun a census form uses, so the definition names the class the answer belongs to.

clue.text: Racket stuck in rectum of long-suffering type?

parts.note: to stick a thing somewhere is to put it there
what goes into a rectum goes up it, which is the only direction on offer
Job of the Old Testament bore calamity after calamity without complaint, so his name is the byword for patience under suffering

explanation.surface: Something shoved where the most patient man in scripture would least want it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries the biblical reference: Job is one particular sufferer, not a type of person. 'Racket' at the front is the swindle, not the noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A put-up job is a swindle arranged in advance between the people running it, and racket carries the same sense of a crooked scheme worked for profit.

clue.text: Drink English rum initially as a depressant

parts.note: to down a pint is to drink it off in one

indicators.note: What happens initially happens first, so only the opening letter of the word beside it is taken.

parts.note: E is the standard letter for English
the first letter of the spirit

explanation.surface: Knocking back a first tot of English rum to take the edge off.
explanation.walkthrough: Drink is the verb here, something you do to a glass rather than what stands in it. Rum looks like more of the same and gives up nothing but its opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A downer is street slang for a sedative or barbiturate, the pill that brings you down, which is what a depressant does.

clue.text: Jail gets Stephen to cook quickish?

parts.note: stir is old prison slang for jail, as in doing five years in stir
Stephen Fry, the British comedian, actor and broadcaster

explanation.surface: A spell inside turns Stephen into a short-order chef.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter conceding that 'quickish' is his own way of putting it rather than a dictionary's. Stir for prison comes from old thieves' cant and survives almost nowhere else in English.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir-fry is to cook in a searing pan with the food kept moving, which is about as quick as cooking gets.

clue.text: Abuse from Peter out to crush a Brit production

indicators.note: To crush a thing is to close on it from both sides, so the letters already found wrap round what comes next.
A production is a fresh staging worked up out of existing material, so those letters come out in an order of their own.

parts.note: to peter out is to die away to nothing; the word parts after its second letter
the five letters in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Peter's energy failing just as he sets about flattening some British show.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter is a man's name in the surface and half a phrasal verb in the wordplay, where to peter out is to fade away and so to die. 'Production' is the shuffling word, the one that makes something new of what it is handed.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a sustained tirade against somebody, so it is abuse delivered at length rather than in a single shout.

clue.text: Went out with old hat

definitions.meaning: the first definition, in the past tense

explanation.surface: An evening out in a hat that has seen better days.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing marks where one definition stops and the other starts, and the clue is five words long with no letters to collect. The past tense of the first half is the only guide to how the answer ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To date someone is to go out with them, in the past tense; and what is dated has fallen out of fashion, which is what old hat means.

clue.text: (&15ac.) How a young impressionable Lewinsky saw Clinton's Trumpian piece of legislation?

parts.words: How a young impressionable Lewinsky saw
parts.note: the impression a star-struck young intern is supposed to have formed of what she was shown
Clinton's first name

explanation.surface: A star-struck intern's memory of the president she was taken with.
explanation.walkthrough: Two presidents are run into one sentence: the last word is Bill Clinton's first name, and the whole answer is Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025. Monica Lewinsky was the White House intern of the 1998 scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act is the tax-and-spending law Trump put his name to, so the answer is that piece of legislation with the Act left off.

clue.text: A place for the football manager: "tit should get fired!"

definitions.text: A place for the football manager

parts.note: a dug is the teat on a cow's or a sow's udder, which is what the blunt word means here
a man who gets fired is out, out of a job and out of the building

explanation.surface: A shout from the terraces that some useless individual ought to be sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tit' is the insult in the surface and the farmyard noun in the wordplay. The quotation marks let the abuse run to the end of the clue, so the definition has to be everything before them.
explanation.definitionFit: The dugout is the sunken shelter beside a football pitch where the manager and his substitutes sit through the game.

clue.text: Tutor in street goes around vehicle to get end away

parts.note: the word taken as it stands

indicators.note: What goes around a thing encircles it, so the street's two letters open up and the shortened vehicle sits inside them.

parts.note: ST is street on any road sign, and the two letters part to take the vehicle between them

indicators.note: The end of a word is its last letter, and getting it away means losing it.

parts.note: a truck is a vehicle, and it is the one whose remains fit
the end letter of TRUCK, which goes

explanation.surface: A tutor hanging about in the street round a van, hoping for a quick one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get your end away' is British slang for having sex, which is what keeps the last four words reading as part of somebody's evening rather than as an instruction to drop a letter. Tutor is the verb, not the man.
explanation.definitionFit: To instruct someone is to teach them, which is what a tutor is paid to do.

clue.text: Brown: "Like to be surrounded by drink"

indicators.note: To be surrounded is to have something on every side, so this piece goes inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits; the word opens after its second letter
as is the word that says one thing is like another

explanation.surface: Brown quoted as wanting nothing better than to be surrounded by drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the capital make Brown look like a surname being quoted; it is the verb a grill performs on bread. Toast is something you drink as well, which is the joke the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: To toast bread is to brown it under heat, so brown is the same verb in its kitchen sense.

clue.text: American Rod, athlete smuggler

parts.note: rod is American slang for a handgun, the word of the gangster films
a runner is an athlete, the track-and-field kind

explanation.surface: An American sportsman by the name of Rod.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod is capitalised so that it reads as a first name, and the comma after it is the only join between the two halves of the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunrunner smuggles weapons across borders, so smuggler names the trade with the cargo left unsaid.

clue.text: Hanger-on Pence, collared by DA, needn't change

indicators.note: To be collared is to be seized and held fast, so this letter is gripped inside the shuffled letters round it.
What changes does not stay as it was, so those letters are re-set in another order.

parts.note: the district attorney's two letters and the six of the other word, eight in all re-set, then parted after the second to take the P
p is pence on any British price tag

explanation.surface: Pence seized by a district attorney and told he need alter nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Pence is the American vice-president in the surface and the p of a price tag in the wordplay. 'Needn't' is material for the shuffle rather than an instruction, its apostrophe counting for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dependant lives at somebody else's expense — the word a tax form uses for the relatives on your hands — which is the charge a hanger-on faces.

clue.text: Am I butch, screwed up and unreasonable?

indicators.note: Something screwed up has been crumpled out of shape, and letters treated that way come out in a different order.

parts.note: eight letters for re-setting

explanation.surface: Someone wondering aloud how macho and how difficult they really are.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites you to read the whole line as one anxious enquiry, which is what hides the join between the letters and the definition. 'Screwed up' does duty in the picture too, as a state of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To call a demand a bit much is to say it is more than anyone could fairly ask, which is the sense unreasonable carries.

clue.text: Judgemental type Jack, our floundering party's centre

indicators.note: A man floundering is thrashing about with no order to him, and letters beside the word do the same.

parts.note: J is the jack in a pack of cards
the three letters in a new order

indicators.note: The centre of a word is the letter at its middle, and that single letter is all this takes.

parts.note: the middle letter of PARTY

explanation.surface: Jack losing his footing at the very heart of our party.
explanation.walkthrough: Judgemental is the trap: a juror judges by appointment rather than by temperament. 'Party's centre' is a letter out of a word, not the moderate wing of anybody's organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: A juror is one of the twelve sworn in to weigh evidence and return a verdict, so judging is the office rather than a failing.

clue.text: see 7dn.
Persecuted type working for a bastard?

parts.note: to work for somebody is to work under them
dog is the old word for a worthless or contemptible man, which is what the question mark covers

explanation.surface: Somebody stuck in a job with a horrible boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is all employment and bad temper, and both halves of the answer are ordinary words hiding in that sentence. An underdog takes its name from the dog losing the fight, the one pinned underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: The underdog is the one expected to lose and pushed about by the stronger side, which is the persecuted party in any unequal contest.

clue.text: Play in which a golfer is abused with putter head

indicators.note: A man abused is knocked about, and letters knocked about will not stay in the order they were given.
The head of a word is the letter at its front, and that is the one taken.

parts.note: seven letters for re-setting
the front letter of the club's name

explanation.surface: A golfer taking a beating from someone wielding the business end of a putter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' is the noun, a children's game, and it is the whole definition despite standing alone at the front. The putter's head is its opening letter here, not the lump of metal on the club.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapfrog is the playground game of vaulting over a bent back, so play is the general word for the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Dodgy used car campaign

indicators.note: Something dodgy is not what it ought to be, and letters that are not as they ought to be want reordering.

parts.note: seven letters for re-setting

explanation.surface: A campaign built on one iffy second-hand motor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy' stands exactly where an adjective describing the car belongs, which is why it reads as part of the picture and not as the instruction. The word crusade now covers any determined campaign, the medieval sense long since lent out.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusade is a long campaign pursued with zeal — an anti-smoking crusade is a campaign — so the two nouns swap straight over.

clue.text: Fanatical right gets one to submit

parts.note: R is right, as on a map or in a stage direction
a is one, as a dozen is one dozen
to submit a price for a contract or at auction is to bid

explanation.surface: A right-winger getting somebody else to give in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' is the political wing in the surface and one letter in the wordplay, and 'submit' is the tender rather than the surrender. Rabid belongs first to a dog with rabies; the fanatic is the figure drawn from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabid supporter is one whose enthusiasm has gone well past reason, which is fanatical in its frothing sense.

clue.text: Finally let belt out to go round middle of Max Hastings?

indicators.note: Letters sent out of where they were sitting have to come back in some other arrangement.
To go round something is to encircle it, so the letters gathered so far close over the one that follows.
The middle of a word is its central letter, and with three letters there is only one candidate.

parts.note: four letters for re-setting, which then open to take a letter inside

indicators.note: What comes finally comes at the end, so the last letter of the word beside it is the one used.

parts.note: the last letter of the word, thrown in with the belt
the central letter of the three

explanation.surface: Loosening your belt at last to get it round a well-known historian's waist.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Hastings is a British military historian and newspaper editor, which is why his full name reads as one man. Split it and the surname is the fight of 1066, while the first name gives up a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hastings names the battle of 1066, the one every British schoolchild is taught, so the question mark lets a particular battle stand for battle itself.

clue.text: Stuff China added to currency units

definitions.note: Stuff is a mass noun and materials a plural, but both name the same undifferentiated quantity of matter, and English uses them interchangeably of what a thing is made from.

parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang china plate gives mate, and a londoner keeps only the first word
the rial is the currency of Iran and of Oman

explanation.surface: Chinese goods thrown in with a heap of foreign money.
explanation.walkthrough: China is the country in the surface and a friend in the wordplay, by way of a rhyme most Londoners no longer hear themselves making. 'Stuff' at the front looks like a verb and is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Materials are what a thing is made from, and stuff is the everyday word for the same quantity of matter before anyone has made anything of it.

clue.text: I say — gather round Conservative right wing!

indicators.note: What goes round something closes over it, so the word before this one opens to take the letter that follows.

parts.note: to rally is to gather, as supporters do to a cause; the word opens after its first letter

indicators.note: The right wing of a word is its far end, so only the letter on that flank is wanted.

parts.note: the letter standing at the right-hand end of the word

explanation.surface: An exclamation of astonishment at the Tory hard right closing ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: Conservative usually hands a crossword its C and here is worth nothing but the letter at its other end. The dash marks where the definition stops and the instructions begin.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Really!' is what you say when something has astonished you, the same mild noise of disbelief as 'I say!'

clue.text: Division when Labour leader opens gob

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, and that one letter is all this takes.

parts.note: to gob is British slang for to spit; the word opens after its second letter

indicators.note: To open a thing is to make a gap in it, and the letter just found goes into the gap.

parts.note: the first letter of the party's name

explanation.surface: A party division that starts the moment the leader opens his mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Gob is the mouth in the surface and the verb to spit in the wordplay, British slang doing both jobs. 'Division' is the parliamentary word as well as the plain one, which is why it sits so easily beside Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: A split in a party is a division into factions, the word the papers reach for when a party falls out with itself.

clue.text: Just like the Eye to rubbish A-list celeb's superior air

indicators.note: To rubbish something is to trash it, and letters trashed come out in any order but their own.

parts.note: five letters for the mix, the hyphen counting for nothing

indicators.note: What is superior stands above the rest, so the letter at the top of the word is the one taken.

parts.note: the letter standing at the head of the word
three more letters for the mix

explanation.surface: The magazine doing to a celebrity's lofty manner what it always does.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eye is Private Eye, the magazine this crossword is printed in, so the definition points at its own pages. 'Superior air' is one idea in the surface and two separate pieces in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye exists to mock the people it reports on, so anything just like it is satirical.

clue.text: John Bull's ultimate pair of balls

indicators.note: What is ultimate comes last of all, so the final letter of the word before it is the one wanted.

parts.note: the last letter of the word
two round shapes drawn side by side on the page

explanation.surface: John Bull, England in human form, reduced to a pair of balls.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bull is the stout squire who stands for England in old cartoons, and the name has to be torn in two, half definition and half wordplay. The second half of the clue is drawing letters rather than defining them.
explanation.definitionFit: The john is what Americans call the lavatory and the loo is what the British call it, so the two pieces of slang meet over the same small room.

clue.text: Just heading off for base

indicators.note: Heading off takes the head of a word away, and a word's head is its first letter.

parts.note: what is just is lawful, squarely within the law
the head of LAWFUL is the L, and off it comes

explanation.surface: Someone fair-minded setting off towards a base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as departing and means decapitating. Base is the adjective — low, contemptible — and not the camp the surface is sending anybody to.
explanation.definitionFit: Base conduct is low and despicable, and awful carries the same flat condemnation of it.

clue.text: Cover withdrawn by party's stand-in members

indicators.note: To withdraw is to draw back, so the letters just given are written out backwards.

parts.note: a lid is the cover of a pot, and its three letters are then read the other way about
a party is a do — a works do, a Christmas do — and more than one makes dos

explanation.surface: Stand-ins at somebody's party, with the lid pulled off the whole business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' is the club sense in the surface and the anatomical one in the answer. Nothing in the clue marks the join except the apostrophe, which belongs to the surface and not to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Member is the old polite word for the penis, and a dildo is the substitute that stands in for one, so the definition makes the joke twice over.

clue.text: Horrendous tool — gasp! Aim to put balls on the right side of it

definitions.text: Aim to put balls on the right side of it
definitions.note: The definition describes the thing instead of naming it, with 'it' standing for the answer itself, which is why it runs to a whole clause.

indicators.note: Something horrendous is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state are not in the order they should be.

parts.note: eight letters for re-setting, the dash between them counting for nothing

explanation.surface: A tool so horrendous it draws a gasp, with balls best kept to one side of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tool' and 'balls' make the surface read as anatomy and only one of them is doing any lettering. The right side of the upright is the inside, where a striker wants his shot to pass.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalpost is what a shot must go the correct side of to count, so the definition names the thing by what a player is trying to do about it.
